strengths: The core idea of hierarchically decoupling reconstruction and semantic objectives into shallow vs. deep layers with separate codebooks is clean, well-motivated, and supported by a convincing ablation (Table 3) showing the objectives can become synergistic rather than conflicting (d vs. c).

The tokenizer results are strong: DualToken achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction (rFID 0.54) while nearly matching the original SigLIP-SO400M in zero-shot classification (81.6 vs. 82.1), clearly outperforming VILA-U on both axes (Table 1, Fig. 1).

The controlled LLaVA-1.5 experiment (Table 4) is a good experimental design: it isolates the tokenizer's effect under matched training data/architecture and shows the discrete unified tokenizer even surpasses continuous SigLIP on several benchmarks.

The unified MLLM achieves competitive results with only a 3B LLM (Table 5), beating several larger unified baselines, and the failure case of naively combining two separate tokenizers (Fig. 4, right) directly supports the paper's central thesis.
The paper is generally well written and the comparison to closely related work (VILA-U, TokenFlow, Janus) is clearly articulated.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly states it is unfinished: 'please note that this research is still ongoing, and the final results, complete metrics, and additional technical details may be updated before the final release,' and repeats this in an 'Important Note' after the conclusion. This alone is disqualifying for a completed conference submission — the work is submitted in an incomplete state with metrics that may change.

Text-to-image generation is evaluated only qualitatively (Fig. 4); there are no standard quantitative generation metrics (e.g., FID-30K, GenEval, or zero-shot ImageNet FID for class-conditional generation), making it impossible to verify claims of 'high-quality generation' or to compare fairly against Emu3, Chameleon, Show-o, or VILA-U on generation.

Missing reproducibility details: loss weights λ1, λ2, λ3, codebook sizes (n2, n3), training schedules, batch sizes, and decoder architecture are not specified; the paper is far below the level of detail needed for reproduction.

Some comparisons are not apples-to-apples: DualToken is initialized from SigLIP-SO400M and trained on CC12M, while reconstruction baselines (SBER-MoVQGAN, MoVQGAN, etc.) were trained with different data, objectives, and resolutions; the zero-shot advantage partly derives from SigLIP initialization rather than the proposed method. The ablation helps, but this confound deserves more careful discussion.

The central claim that a unified tokenizer surpasses the combination of two distinct encoders is supported only by qualitative images; no quantitative metric is reported for this key comparison, and it appears only in one figure caption.
There is a likely typo in Eq. (2): 'Lc1 + Lc1' should presumably be 'Lc1 + Lc2', which obscures the total loss formulation.

Novelty is moderate: dual/separate codebooks for semantic and perceptual features already exist (TokenFlow), and the hierarchical shallow/deep layer split is a fairly simple design choice; the main contribution is an empirical observation rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The unified MLLM comparison in Table 5 mixes model scales and training data with limited disclosure of DualToken's own pretraining/instruction-tuning data, weakening the significance of the 3B-vs-7B comparisons.

strengths: The hierarchical decoupling of reconstruction (shallow layers) and semantic (deep layers) objectives is a simple, sensible idea, and Table 3 provides a clean ablation showing the naive joint objective fails while the hierarchical one yields both strong reconstruction (rFID 0.54) and preserved semantics (81.6% zero-shot).

The tokenizer-level results are strong: DualToken outperforms VILA-U substantially and matches or beats dedicated reconstruction tokenizers (e.g., SBER-MoVQGAN) on rFID/PSNR/SSIM while retaining near-SigLIP semantic performance.

The controlled LLaVA-1.5 experiment (Table 4) is a good practice, isolating the tokenizer's effect under fixed training data and LLM, and the comparison of semantic-only vs. semantic+perceptual tokens is informative.
The negative result showing that naively combining SBER-MoVQGAN and VQ'd SigLIP codebooks performs poorly supports the case for a unified tokenizer rather than stitched components.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly states it is work in progress: 'this research is still ongoing, and the final results, complete metrics, and additional technical details may be updated before the final release' (Sections 4 and the Important Note). This is a fundamental disqualification for a conference submission — the evaluation is incomplete and the presented numbers may not be final.

Text-to-image generation is evaluated only qualitatively (Fig. 4); there is no quantitative generation metric (e.g., MS-COCO FID/CLIP score), which is the central claim of a unified generation model. Without it, the generation contribution is unsupported.

Novelty is limited relative to concurrent/related work: TokenFlow [33] already proposes separate codebooks for semantic and texture features; the main differences (single vision tower, layer-wise split with L2 distillation to the pretrained state) are relatively incremental engineering choices rather than a new insight.

Key methodological details are missing or vague: loss weights λ1–λ3 are never specified, codebook sizes are unstated, the choice of layers 6/26 is not ablated, and Eq. (2) contains an apparent typo (Lc1 + Lc1). This severely harms reproducibility.

Comparisons in Table 5 mix model scales and training data inconsistently (DualToken 3B vs. 7B baselines; unknown pretraining/instruction data), making 'comparable to LLaVA-NeXT/ShareGPT4V' claims hard to interpret; some DualToken results (MMVet 32.5) are below several baselines it claims comparability with.

The 'synergy' claim is under-analyzed: the observation that adding a semantic loss improves reconstruction (Table 3 d vs. c) is interesting but no analysis, additional datasets, or seeds are provided to establish it as more than a single-run artifact or regularization effect.

Semantic supervision is only a simple L2 distillation to the frozen pretrained features; it is unclear why this preserves zero-shot retrieval at 21.05/21.55 vs. SigLIP's 21.70/21.60 while classification rises to 81.6 — potential inconsistencies that warrant explanation.

RQ-VAE depth transformers, EMA codebooks, and restart strategies are all standard components; the paper's technical machinery is largely assembled from prior work without justification of design choices.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the conflict between reconstruction and semantic objectives in unified tokenizers is convincingly demonstrated (Table 3a vs. 3b/c).

The hierarchical decoupling idea (shallow layers for reconstruction, deep layers for semantics) is simple, elegant, and the surprising synergy finding—that adding the deep-layer semantic loss improves shallow-layer reconstruction (Table 3d vs. 3c)—is an interesting empirical observation.

Strong tokenizer results: rFID 0.54, PSNR 23.56, SSIM 0.742 outperform dedicated reconstruction tokenizers (SBER-MoVQGAN, Open-MAGVIT2) while retaining near-SigLIP semantic performance (81.6% zero-shot).

Well-controlled downstream experiments: swapping tokenizers within the LLaVA-1.5 framework (Table 4) isolates the tokenizer's effect, and DualToken even surpasses continuous SigLIP; the dual-codebook vs. naive-combination ablation (Fig. 4) directly supports the core design choice.
Unified MLLM results are competitive at 3B parameters against 7B unified models (Table 5), which is a meaningful efficiency point.
weaknesses: The paper explicitly states it is unfinished: 'this research is still ongoing, and the final results, complete metrics, and additional technical details may be updated before the final release.' This is repeated in Table 5 and in an 'Important Note.' Submitting an in-progress manuscript with provisional metrics is not acceptable for a top-tier venue and undermines the validity of all reported numbers.

Quantitative image generation evaluation is entirely missing: generation quality is only shown via cherry-picked qualitative examples (Fig. 4). Standard metrics (e.g., GenEval, MJHQ-FID, or text-to-image FID on a held-out set) are needed to support the claim of 'high-quality generation.'

Novelty is incremental relative to closely related concurrent work. TokenFlow [33] also uses separate semantic/texture codebooks, and VILA-U [46] already pursues a unified semantic+reconstruction tokenizer; the main delta is applying losses at different ViT depths, which is a relatively straightforward architectural choice. Differentiation from TokenFlow, while discussed, is not empirically compared head-to-head.

Key training details are absent: loss weights (λ1, λ2, λ3), codebook sizes (n2, n3), restart strategy parameters, training epochs/throughput, and pretraining/instruction-tuning data mixture are unspecified, hurting reproducibility.

The layer selection (layers 1-6 for reconstruction, layer 26 for semantics) appears ad hoc with no ablation over alternative depth splits, and there is no analysis explaining *why* the semantic objective improves shallow-layer reconstruction (the central 'synergy' claim is asserted, not investigated).
Table 5 comparisons across unified models with different training data, resolutions, and scales are not apples-to-apples; only the LLaVA-1.5 controlled experiment is truly fair.

Writing/polish issues: Eq. 2 contains a typo (L_c1 + L_c1), references [41]/[42] are duplicates, and several typos ('singe MLLM', 'appears' vs. 'appear'), suggesting the manuscript was not carefully prepared.

The semantic loss is a simple L2 distillation to the initial pretrained state rather than contrastive alignment; the claim that this preserves language alignment is supported only by zero-shot accuracy and Flickr8K retrieval on a small dataset—broader semantic evaluation is warranted.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: decoupling reconstruction and semantic objectives via separate pixel and semantic codebooks applied to shallow vs. deep ViT layers, which directly addresses a documented conflict in unified tokenizers (validated empirically in Table 2 and Table 3).

Strong and convincing tokenizer results: state-of-the-art among unified tokenizers on both reconstruction (rFID 0.25, PSNR, SSIM) and semantics (82.0% zero-shot on ImageNet), and a fair like-for-like comparison against UniTok under matched encoder/decoder settings (Table 10) showing consistent gains.

Well-controlled downstream evaluations: within LLaVA-1.5, DualToken surpasses both VILA-U and the original continuous SigLIP; in the unified MLLM setting, a reproduced VILA-U with the same backbone/data/training recipe is included for fairness.

Interesting and useful analysis beyond raw numbers: pixel tokens improving understanding (Table 4), semantic tokens improving generation (Table 5b), UMAP analysis explaining why a unified tokenizer beats dual heterogeneous encoders, and computational overhead analysis (Table 11).

Thorough ablations and generalization studies in the appendix: layer selection across six backbones and multiple model sizes, robustness to layer choice, and complementary results with advanced quantizers (MCQ).
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: separate codebooks for semantics vs. appearance exist in TokenFlow, FQGAN's factorized tokenization, and Illume+'s dual visual tokenization; the main distinction (hierarchical feature split within a single vision tower) is a natural extension, and the semantic loss is essentially a simple feature distillation to the pretrained SigLIP weights.

A portion of the semantic performance likely derives from the increasingly strong pretrained backbones (SigLIP/SigLIP2), so improvements must be read through the controlled comparisons rather than absolute numbers; the paper would benefit from even more emphasis on this.

Some evaluation details limit strict comparability: token depth D=8 vs. VILA-U's D=16 at 384px, comparisons to concurrent works trained on different data mixtures, and in-house data in training stages that is not publicly verifiable.
Presentation issues: typos in text ('inherently conflict', 'singe MLLM') and in Eq. 2 (the commitment loss term appears twice as L_c1), which suggests insufficient proofreading.
Generation evaluation, while broad (GenAI-Bench, MJHQ, GenEval, WISE), relies heavily on VQAScore-style automatic judges whose reliability is debated; human evaluation is absent.

strengths: Comprehensive tokenizer-level evaluation across semantic (zero-shot, retrieval) and reconstruction (rFID, PSNR, SSIM) metrics, compared against dedicated reconstruction-only and understanding-only models (Table 1).
Controlled downstream experiments in the LLaVA-1.5 framework (Table 4) isolate the effect of the tokenizer on understanding, and the Sem-only vs Sem+Pix ablation is informative.
The dual-encoder vs unified-tokenizer comparison (Table 6, Appendix F.4) with UMAP visualization addresses a fundamental design question with a reasonably controlled setup.

Appendix provides breadth: layer-selection robustness across six backbones (Tables 7-9), UniTok/MCQ integration (Table 10), computational overhead analysis, GenEval/WISE results, and training data details.
The motivation experiment (Table 2) formally validating that reconstruction-trained encoders underperform in MLLMs is a useful empirical contribution.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: separate codebooks for appearance vs semantics have been explored (TokenFlow's shared-mapping, FQGAN's factorized codebook, Janus, Illume+ dual tokenization), and the shallow-vs-deep layer observation is explicitly supported by prior work (Chen et al., 2025a). The main new element—applying reconstruction loss to shallow layers and distilling semantics at the last layer—is an engineering recombination rather than a conceptual advance.

The 'semantic' capability is largely inherited for free: the semantic loss (Eq. 4) is a distillation to the pretrained SigLIP initial state. The paper's claim of resolving the conflict is somewhat overstated—it preserves CLIP semantics via anchoring rather than learning semantics, which weakens the framing of the contribution.

Key methodological details are missing or inconsistent: loss weights λ1, λ2, λ3 in Eq. 2 are never specified; Eq. 2 contains an apparent typo (L_c1 + L_c1); the depth-transformer tokenization/head details are spread thinly across Sec. 3.3 and Appendix F.4, hurting reproducibility.

Evidence that semantic tokens promote generation is weaker than claimed: the quantitative support is a single ablation (DualToken-3B pix-only vs. full on GenAI-Bench, Table 5b) plus qualitative Figure 5; there is no analysis of how semantic tokens are consumed by the decoder (pixel tokens alone are decoded) or whether the benefit is simply a regularization effect from doubled supervision.

Understanding comparisons in Table 5 are confounded: different training data recipes, resolutions, and in-house data across baselines make the 5.8-point average improvement claim over VILA-U and 'surpasses LLaVA-NeXT' statements difficult to attribute to the tokenizer alone.

Several claimed SOTA statements are shaky: MJHQ FID (Table 6) is worse than Janus (7.88 vs 10.10 aside, but Liquid achieves 5.47), GenEval (0.75) trails Janus-Pro-7B (0.80), and WISE (0.39) only matches Emu3 and Show-o2; 'state-of-the-art in both tasks among discrete AR models' is stronger than the evidence.

Generation efficiency claims are under-analyzed: predicting both pixel and semantic residual tokens per position doubles the visual-head prediction work and lengthens generation; the overhead analysis (Appendix D) focuses on memory/FLOPs of the tokenizer but does not clearly quantify generation-time cost or the benefit/cost tradeoff of semantic tokens at inference.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core idea: instead of forcing a single visual vocabulary to serve both reconstruction and semantic objectives (which the paper convincingly shows conflict), DualToken decouples them into a pixel codebook on shallow layers and a semantic codebook on deep layers of a unified SigLIP-initialized ViT. The design is simple, elegant, and well-grounded in the observed layer-wise cosine similarity structure.

Strong empirical results for a unified tokenizer: best-in-class rFID (0.25) and PSNR/SSIM among unified tokenizers while surpassing or matching dedicated reconstruction models, and 82.0% zero-shot accuracy on ImageNet surpassing dedicated semantic models like CLIP-L/14-336. Achieves this with roughly 10% of the pretraining data used by VILA-U.

Well-designed, convincing evaluation: (i) a controlled preliminary experiment (Table 2) formally validating that reconstruction-trained encoders hurt MLLM understanding; (ii) a careful ablation (Table 3) isolating the conflict (a vs b vs c vs d); (iii) controlled LLaVA-1.5 comparisons against VILA-U and SigLIP across ten benchmarks; (iv) a reproduced VILA-U baseline under an identical 3B backbone and training recipe for the unified model; (v) an apples-to-apples dual-encoder baseline (Table 6 / Appendix F.4) that directly tests the 'unified tokenizer vs. two heterogeneous encoders' question, supported by UMAP feature-space analysis.

Interesting and useful findings beyond the main result: pixel tokens improve understanding (e.g., OCRB +2.9, POPE +2.7 in Table 4), and semantic tokens act as positive supervision during generation (pix.-only ablation drops 0.13 on GenAI-Bench overall), with qualitative examples supporting both.

Good generalization and robustness evidence: the layer-partition heuristic is validated across six backbones (CLIP, DFN, EVA, SigLIP, SigLIP2, ViTamin) and multiple scales (Tables 7-9), plus a fair re-trained comparison with UniTok showing complementarity (Table 10).

Practical considerations addressed: computational analysis (Appendix D) shows the dual-token design adds only ~9% parameters and ~13% inference latency via embedding-dimension concatenation rather than longer sequences; extended generation evaluation (GenEval, WISE, MJHQ) in the appendix.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: separate codebooks for semantics vs. appearance have been explored (TokenFlow's shared-mapping dual codebooks, FQGAN's factorized/divide-and-conquer codebooks), and layer-wise shallow/deep feature specialization in ViTs is well documented. The contribution is primarily a well-executed recombination plus the observation that anchoring the final layer to its pretrained state suffices—valuable but incremental in design.

Cross-method comparisons in Tables 5 and 12 involve varying resolutions (256px vs 384px vs 432px), parameter counts, and training data; while the reproduced VILA-U baseline mitigates this for the tokenizer question, headline numbers could overstate superiority over e.g. Janus-Pro-7B (GenEval 0.80 vs 0.75) and Show-o2-7B, whose training recipes differ substantially.

The semantic objective is simply a feature-space anchor to the frozen initial state (Eq. 4) with no contrastive/CLIP-style loss; it is surprising this preserves text alignment, and the paper offers little analysis of why or of potential failure modes on distributions far from the pretraining data.

Minor presentation issues that should be fixed: typo in Eq. 2 (L_c1 + L_c1 should be L_c1 + L_c2), several grammatical errors ('inherently conflict', 'a singe MLLM', 'Semantic tokens also helps'), and the paper leans on in-house datasets (2M VQA data, in-house IFT/aesthetics data) limiting full reproducibility of the downstream MLLM results.
